FAQs

These are some of the Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best English support for international and bilingual school students in Thảo Điền?

The most effective support targets academic English—reading comprehension, structured writing, and curriculum-aligned skills—rather than general conversation. Spark English specialises in helping students from both international and bilingual schools succeed in their specific school environment.

What does “premium English learning experience” mean?

At Spark, premium means small class sizes (maximum 4 students), personalised learning plans, a structured curriculum aligned with international standards, and measurable progress. Students receive focused, expert attention that produces faster and more lasting results.

Do students from Vinschool or Asian School need extra English support?

Yes. Many bilingual school students can communicate in English but lack the academic skills needed for advanced reading, structured essay writing, and grammar accuracy. Targeted support helps them perform significantly better in English-medium subjects and examinations.

How is Spark different from centres like ILA or VUS?

Spark focuses exclusively on academic English support and IELTS preparation, not general communication classes. Our programmes are designed around the specific demands of international and bilingual school curricula, with expert teachers who understand IB, British, and Vietnamese bilingual systems.

What IELTS score can students achieve at Spark?

Students progress through structured levels: from Band 4.5 to 6.5+ at the foundation and intermediate stages, and from 7.0 to 8.5+ at advanced and elite levels. One of our founders has achieved an IELTS band score of 9.0 multiple times and brings that expertise directly into our teaching methodology.

How long does it take to see improvement?

Most students show noticeable progress within 8 to 12 weeks for reading and writing skills. Significant academic improvement typically occurs within 3 to 6 months of consistent attendance.

Do you support school homework and writing assignments?

Yes. Our Academic English Support programme is designed to help students with their actual schoolwork—completing assignments, improving essays, and understanding class materials more effectively

What age groups do you teach?

We welcome students from age 3 and above. Our Phonics and Literacy programme serves the youngest learners, while our Academic English and IELTS tracks support primary and secondary students through to university preparation.

Is IELTS preparation available in Thảo Điền?

Yes. Spark offers a complete IELTS program right in Thảo Điền, covering every level from foundation through to high-band mastery. Our structured approach includes academic writing, critical thinking, and proven exam strategies.

What is the difference between ESL and academic English?

ESL (English as a Second Language) focuses on general communication skills. Academic English goes further—it develops the reading comprehension, essay writing, analytical thinking, and vocabulary needed to succeed in an English-medium school environment. Spark addresses both, depending on each student's needs.

How do I know if my child needs extra English support?

Common signs include: slow or reluctant reading, difficulty writing sentences or paragraphs, low confidence during class discussions, and taking significantly longer than expected to complete homework. If you notice any of these, a professional assessment is recommended.

Where is Spark English Center located?

Spark English Center Vietnam is located in Thảo Điền, Ho Chi Minh City. Our centre is close to major international and bilingual schools as well as popular residential developments in the area.

Do you offer an assessment before enrollment?

Yes. Every student begins with a free, comprehensive English assessment. This provides a clear diagnosis of their current level, identifies specific areas for improvement, and results in a personalized learning plan with defined goals.

Can Spark help with study-abroad preparation?

Absolutely. Our IELTS program and Academic English tracks are specifically designed to prepare students for international university admission. We help students achieve the English proficiency and academic writing skills required by universities worldwide.

How are students placed into the right class?

Every student completes a free assessment evaluating reading, writing, and overall academic English ability. Based on the results, we place them in a class that matches their level—not just their age—so they can progress effectively.

What happens in a typical lesson at Spark?

Each lesson is structured and focused. Students work on reading comprehension, writing tasks, vocabulary development, and grammar in context. Lessons are designed to build real academic skills, not just complete activities.

Will my child improve their writing skills?

Yes. Writing is a core focus at Spark. Students learn how to:

  • Organize ideas clearly
  • Write structured paragraphs and essays
  • Use accurate grammar and vocabulary

This leads to noticeable improvement in both school assignments and exams.

Do students receive feedback on their work?

Yes. Students receive detailed, ongoing feedback on their writing, reading, and overall performance. This helps them understand their mistakes and improve quickly.

How do you ensure students stay motivated?

We combine clear progress tracking, achievable goals, and engaging lessons. Students feel motivated because they can see real improvement in their school performance.

Are classes suitable for shy or less confident students?

Yes. Small class sizes create a safe, supportive environment where students feel comfortable participating, asking questions, and building confidence.

What if my child is already strong in English?

Many strong students still lack advanced academic skills, especially in writing and critical thinking. Spark helps them move from “good” to top-performing, including high IELTS bands.

How often should students attend classes?

We typically recommend 2–3 sessions per week for consistent progress. For IELTS or urgent improvement, a more intensive schedule may be advised.

Can Spark help students catch up quickly?

Yes. With focused instruction and small classes, students can close gaps efficiently, especially in reading and writing. Progress depends on consistency and effort.

Do you give homework?

Yes. Homework is purposeful and reinforces lesson content. It helps students practice skills independently and accelerate their progress.

How do parents stay informed about progress?

Parents receive regular updates and feedback, including insights into strengths, areas for improvement, and next steps.

What curriculum does Spark follow?

Spark uses a structured, internally developed curriculum aligned with international standards and adapted to IB, Cambridge, and bilingual school requirements.

Are lessons taught by native English teachers?

Spark focuses on expert teachers with strong academic English teaching experience, not just native speakers. The priority is teaching quality and results.

What class times are available?

We offer flexible scheduling, including after-school and weekend classes, to fit around students' school commitments.

Is there a trial class available?

Students begin with a free assessment, and in many cases can experience a lesson to ensure the class is the right fit before committing.

What makes Spark effective compared to private tutoring?

Spark offers both small-group classes and one-to-one tutoring, depending on each student's needs.

What results can parents expect long-term?

Students develop:

  • Strong reading comprehension
  • Clear, structured writing
  • Academic vocabulary
  • Confidence in English-medium learning

These skills support long-term academic success, not just short-term improvement.

In short

Our story, in four facts

  • Founded in 2019 in Thao Dien, Ho Chi Minh City.
  • Maximum six students per class — a hard limit, not an average.
  • MOET-licensed and independently operated. No franchise, no corporate curriculum.
  • Four structured programs: Phonics, ESL, Academic English and IELTS preparation.

About Us

Spark English Center Vietnam is a premium English learning center in Thao Dien, Ho Chi Minh City. We support students at international and bilingual schools across HCMC with structured, results-driven programs in Phonics, ESL, Academic English, and IELTS preparation.

We keep classes small. Maximum six students. Every student gets a personalized learning plan. Every lesson is structured around measurable progress, not just activity.

We are MOET-licensed and independently operated. No franchise. No corporate curriculum. Just experienced teachers, proven methods, and a genuine commitment to each child's growth.

How Spark Started

Spark was founded in 2019 with a simple observation: too many children at good schools were still struggling with English.

Not because they lacked ability. Because nobody had taken the time to find the specific gap and close it properly.

Parents were spending money on large-class centers where their child was one of twenty. Or cycling through private tutors who helped with homework but never built the underlying skills. Progress was slow, inconsistent, or invisible. Spark was built to fix that.

We started with a small group of students and one clear principle: assess first, teach second. Find out exactly where a child is. Build a plan around what they actually need. Keep the class small enough that the teacher can see every mistake, correct every misunderstanding, and celebrate every step forward.

That principle has not changed. Today, Spark serves students from over a dozen international and bilingual schools across Ho Chi Minh City, from early phonics learners to IELTS candidates preparing for international university admissions.

What Makes Spark Different

Six Things That Set Us Apart

Maximum 6 Students Per Class

This is not a marketing number. It is a hard limit. Research shows that meaningful individual feedback drops sharply beyond six students. We enforce this because it is the foundation of everything we do.

Diagnostic Process Assessment Before Everything

Every student begins with a free, comprehensive English assessment. We evaluate reading, writing, speaking, and listening. We identify specific gaps. We build a personalized learning plan before the first lesson begins.

Structured Programs, Not Generic Classes

We do not offer "general English conversation." Our four core programs, Phonics and Early Literacy, ESL Foundations, Academic English, and IELTS Preparation, are each built around specific learning outcomes with clear progression milestones.

MOET-Licensed and Independently Operated

Spark holds a full MOET teaching license through our registered Vietnamese entity. We are not a franchise or branch of a larger chain. Every decision about curriculum, teaching methods, and class structure is made here, for the students in front of us.

Aligned with International School Curricula

Our teachers understand IB, Cambridge, and Vietnamese bilingual curricula. We do not teach in isolation. We build the reading, writing, and critical thinking skills students need to succeed in their actual school environment.

Real Results, Tracked and Shared

Parents receive regular progress updates through ClassDojo and quarterly parent meetings via Zoom. We track improvement, share it clearly, and adjust plans as students grow.

Meet The Team

The People Behind Spark

Our Programs

From First Sounds to University Ready

Spark offers four structured programs that together form a complete English learning pathway

British International School (BIS), International School of Ho Chi Minh City (ISHCMC), Australian International School (AIS), Vinschool, Asian School, EtonHouse, Aurora International School, Saigon South International School (SSIS), ABC International School, and The American School (TAS).

We are not affiliated with any school. We are an independent support center that works alongside schools to help students reach their full potential.

FAQs

Frequently Asked Questions About Spark English Center Vietnam

What is Spark English Center Vietnam?

Spark English Center Vietnam is a MOET-licensed, premium English learning center in Thao Dien, Ho Chi Minh City. We specialize in small-class instruction (maximum 6 students) for children and teenagers attending international and bilingual schools. Our programs cover Phonics, ESL, Academic English, and IELTS preparation.

Where is Spark English Center located?

Spark is located at 204B7/12 Nguyen Van Huong, Thao Dien Ward, Ho Chi Minh City. We are within walking or short driving distance of BIS, ISHCMC, AIS, EtonHouse, Aurora, and other international schools in the Thao Dien and District 2 area.

Is Spark English Center MOET-licensed?

Yes. Spark holds a full MOET (Ministry of Education and Training) teaching license. We are an independently operated, fully registered educational center in Vietnam, not a franchise or branch of a larger chain.

What ages does Spark English Center accept?

Spark welcomes students from age 3 and above. Our Phonics and Early Literacy program serves the youngest learners (ages 3-7). ESL Foundations covers ages 7-12. Academic English supports ages 10-16. IELTS Preparation is available for students aged 14 and above.

What is the class size at Spark?

Maximum 6 students per class. This is a hard limit, not an average. We enforce this because research shows that meaningful individual feedback and correction drops sharply beyond six students. Small classes allow our teachers to see every mistake, adjust every plan, and give each student the attention they need.

Who is the IELTS instructor at Spark?

Joe Evans is the Director and lead IELTS instructor at Spark English Center Vietnam. He holds an MBA and MS from Texas Tech University and a TEFL Masters Certification. With over six years of specialized IELTS teaching, he focuses on Academic IELTS, particularly Writing and Speaking. Over 95% of his students achieve Band 7.5 or higher.

What IELTS band score can students achieve at Spark?

Students progress through four structured levels: Entry (Band 4.5-5.5), Intermediate (Band 5.5-6.5), Advanced (Band 7.0-8.0), and Elite (Band 8.5-9.0). Over 95% of IELTS students at Spark achieve Band 7.5 or higher under Joe Evans' instruction.

How is Spark different from large English centers like ILA, VUS, or DOL?

Spark is not a factory. We keep classes at a maximum of 6 students. We focus exclusively on academic English support and IELTS preparation, not general conversation classes. Our programs are designed around the specific demands of international and bilingual school curricula, with teachers who understand IB, Cambridge, and Vietnamese bilingual systems. Every student receives a personalized learning plan.

How is Spark different from a private tutor?

Private tutors typically help with homework but rarely build the underlying skills a student is missing. Spark provides structured curriculum, clear progression milestones, peer learning in a small group, progress tracking, and quarterly parent meetings. It is systematic skill development, not session-by-session support.

Do you offer a free assessment?

Yes. Every student begins with a free, comprehensive English assessment covering reading, writing, speaking, and listening. After the assessment, parents receive a detailed report with their child's current level, identified gaps, and a recommended learning plan. There is no obligation to enroll.

How do parents track their child's progress at Spark?

Teachers communicate with parents directly through ClassDojo. Spark also holds quarterly parent meetings via Zoom, a 20-minute one-on-one call every three months to discuss progress, challenges, and strategies for supporting learning at home.

Does Spark help with international school homework and assignments?

Yes. Our Academic English program is designed to help students with their actual schoolwork: completing assignments, improving essays, and understanding class materials more effectively.

We work alongside, not against, what students are learning at school.

Can Spark help my child prepare for international university admissions?

Yes. Our IELTS program and Academic English tracks are specifically designed to prepare students for international university admission. We help students achieve the English proficiency and academic writing skills required by universities in the UK, US, Australia, Canada, and beyond.

What is the difference between ESL and Academic English?

ESL (English as a Second Language) focuses on building general communication skills from the ground up, ideal for students who are still developing basic English fluency. Academic English goes further: it develops the reading comprehension, structured essay writing, analytical thinking, and subject-specific vocabulary needed to succeed in an English-medium school environment. Many students need to transition from ESL to Academic English as their fluency grows.

What phonics method does Spark use?

Spark uses systematic, evidence-based phonics instruction. We teach children to decode English from individual letter sounds through blending, segmenting, and reading connected text. Our program is aligned with Cambridge YLE standards and uses materials including Fun for Starters, Movers, and Flyers. This approach gives children the tools to read independently rather than relying on memorization or guessing.

How long does it take to see improvement?

Most students show noticeable progress within 8 to 12 weeks for reading and writing skills. Significant academic improvement, including better school grades and teacher feedback, typically occurs within 3 to 6 months of consistent attendance.

Do you offer sibling discounts or referral programs?

Yes. Siblings are eligible for a 5% discount on class fees. Families also receive a one-time 10% referral discount on the first month's enrollment fee for every new student they refer who enrolls in a quarterly program. There is no cap on referrals.

What are Spark's operating hours and location?

Spark is open Monday through Saturday. Classes are available from morning to evening with flexible scheduling. We are located at 204B7/12 Nguyen Van Huong, Thao Dien Ward, Ho Chi Minh City. To inquire or book an assessment, call 0398143487 or email sparkalcvn@gmail.com.

6 years. Hundreds of students. 95% at Band 7.5 or above.

Joe Evans is Spark's Director and lead IELTS instructor. He specializes in Academic IELTS and has helped students at every level, from Band 4.5 beginners to candidates pushing for Band 8.5 and above, achieve the scores their futures depend on.

What Joe brings to every lesson

  • 6+ years of focused IELTS instruction, specializing in Academic IELTS
  • 95% of students achieve Band 7.5 or higher
  • Specialist focus on Writing and Speaking — the skills Vietnamese students lose the most points on
  • Detailed personalized feedback on every written task
  • Tailored study plans from the first lesson, built around each student's target score and timeline
  • Regular mock tests under timed conditions with full examiner-style assessment
  • Complete IELTS materials including Cambridge Official Practice Tests

More about us

Teaching philosophy

Why Joe's Students Succeed

Joe's approach to teaching is rooted in a simple belief: every student can improve with the right guidance and a clear plan. Too often, students become frustrated because they are working hard without seeing results. They complete practice tests, memorize vocabulary lists, and study for hours, yet still struggle to reach their target score.

Rather than focusing on shortcuts, Joe helps students understand the skills behind success. He breaks complex tasks into manageable steps, provides detailed feedback, and teaches students how to identify and correct their own mistakes. This not only leads to stronger IELTS results but also builds confidence and long-term language skills.

By combining structure, accountability, and personalized support, Joe creates a learning environment where students can make consistent progress and develop the confidence needed to perform at their best on exam day.

Joe's Approach is Built on Three Things

Consistency

Band scores improve through deliberate, regular practice, not cramming. Joe builds study schedules students can actually sustain, and holds them to it.

Deliberate practice

Every Writing task is treated as a craft exercise. Argument structure, task achievement, lexical range, grammatical accuracy: each element is taught, practiced, and refined in isolation before being put together under exam conditions.

Personalized support

No two students have the same weaknesses. Joe identifies exactly where each student is losing points and works on those gaps specifically, not a generic course that treats everyone the same.

Student Success Stories

Joe has helped hundreds of students achieve the IELTS scores they need for university admissions, international study programs, immigration applications, and professional opportunities. His students come from a wide range of backgrounds and ability levels, but they all share one goal: improving their English and achieving their target score.

One recent student joined the course with an overall Band 5.5 and struggled particularly with Writing Task 2. Through structured lessons, detailed feedback, and a personalized study plan, the student gradually improved their writing organization, grammatical accuracy, and argument development. After four months of focused preparation, they achieved an overall Band 7.5, exceeding their original target score.

Another student had taken the IELTS exam twice without reaching the score required for university admission. By identifying specific weaknesses in Speaking and Writing and focusing on deliberate practice, they were able to improve their confidence and performance significantly. On their next attempt, they achieved the score needed to move forward with their academic plans.

These success stories are not the result of shortcuts or memorized templates. They reflect the consistent effort of motivated students combined with clear guidance, targeted feedback, and a proven teaching approach. Joe's goal is to help every student understand exactly what they need to improve and provide the support necessary to reach their full potential.

FAQs

Choosing the right IELTS course is an important decision, and it's natural to have questions before getting started. Whether you're preparing for university admission, immigration, professional registration, or simply aiming for a higher score, understanding the learning process can help you make an informed choice. Below are answers to some of the most common questions students ask about Joe's teaching approach, course structure, and what to expect throughout their IELTS journey.

How long does it take to improve my IELTS score?

Every student starts at a different level. Joe does not guess your target—he assesses your current band in the first session and gives you a clear, realistic pathway. Most students working consistently with Joe achieve Band 7.5 or higher, with many improving 1–2 full bands within a few months.

How long does it take to improve my IELTS score?

It depends on your starting point and your target.

  • Band 5.5 → 6.5: ~6–10 weeks
  • Band 6.0 → 7.0+: ~8–12 weeks
  • Band 6.5 → 7.5+: focused refinement

The key is not time alone—it's structured practice + feedback, which is where most students fail without guidance.

Why focus so much on Writing and Speaking?

Because this is where most students lose the most points.

Listening and Reading can improve with practice tests. Writing and Speaking require:

  • Structure
  • Vocabulary control
  • Clear thinking under pressure

These are the skills that move students from Band 6 → Band 7.5+.

How is this different from other IELTS courses?

Most courses:

  • Teach general tips
  • Use large classes
  • Give limited feedback

Joe's approach is different:

  • Small groups or personalized attention
  • Detailed correction on every writing task
  • Specific feedback on exactly where you lose marks
  • Study plan tailored to your target score

You are not following a course. The course is built around you.

Do I need a strong English foundation before joining?

No. Joe has worked with students from:

  • Band 4.5 beginners
  • Up to Band 8+ advanced candidates

What matters is not your starting level—it's your willingness to follow the system consistently.

How often will I receive feedback?

Every writing task is reviewed in detail. You will receive:

  • Corrections on grammar and vocabulary
  • Structural improvements
  • Band-level feedback
  • Clear instructions on what to fix next

This is where most score improvements come from.

Will I take mock tests?

Yes. Students regularly complete:

  • Full timed mock tests
  • Section-based practice
  • Examiner-style scoring

This ensures you are fully prepared for real test conditions.

Is this suitable for students in international schools?

Yes—this is exactly who the program is designed for. Many international school students:

  • Understand English well
  • But struggle with academic writing and structured speaking

Joe focuses specifically on these gaps.

What if I've taken IELTS before and didn't improve?

This is common. Most students plateau because:

  • They repeat practice tests
  • Without fixing underlying weaknesses

Joe identifies exactly why your score is stuck and focuses only on what needs to change.

Is this the right time to start?

Book a free IELTS assessment. In this session, Joe will:

  • Estimate your current band
  • Identify your biggest weaknesses
  • Recommend a clear plan to reach your target score

No guesswork. No generic advice.

How do I get started?

If you have a target score and a timeline—yes. The earlier you start, the more time you have to:

  • Build real skill
  • Avoid last-minute pressure
  • Improve your final result

pages.content:
In short

This guide in three steps

  • Step 1: get clear on what you actually need — the problem, your timeline and your budget.
  • Step 2: understand your three real options — large chains, specialist small-group centers, private tutors.
  • Step 3: evaluate on class size, teacher specialism, diagnostic process, curriculum alignment, progress reporting, trial and pricing.
  • Self-assessment: ten questions to ask any center before booking.

Choosing the Right English Support for Your Child

Choosing an English center for an international or bilingual school child in HCMC is harder than it should be. The big chains advertise everywhere, the smaller centers are not always easy to find, the private tutors operate by word of mouth, and almost nobody in the category will give you an honest comparison. Most centers want you to book a sales call so they can pitch. Most reviews online are either anonymous complaints or paid placements. Parents are left to make a consequential decision with surprisingly little reliable information.

This guide is our attempt to give parents the framework we wish was available when we started Spark. We are an English center ourselves, in Thao Dien, focused on international and bilingual school families. We have a clear interest in your child being a good fit for us. But we have written this honestly enough that you should be able to use it to evaluate any center, including ours, and even to walk away from us if the framework points elsewhere. We would rather you find the right English support than the closest one.

A note before we begin

The honest answer to "what is the best English center in HCMC" is not a name. It is a fit. The right English center for a Year 2 child needing phonics is different from the right one for a Year 11 child preparing for IGCSE English Literature. The right answer for a Korean transfer student starting at AIS is different from the right answer for a Vietnamese family at Vinschool. The framework below helps you find your fit. The brand names are secondary.

Step 1

Get Clear on What You Actually Need

Before evaluating any center, take an hour to clarify what you are solving for. Most parents skip this step and end up evaluating options against an unclear target.

Which child is yours?

Five common reasons international school families seek outside English support. The right center for each is different.

01

The struggling child

School reports show "below expectations" in English. The child cannot keep pace with classroom demands.

What you needA center that can diagnose accurately, group rigorously and rebuild specific skills. Class size, methodology and teacher quality all matter.

02

The plateaued child

Early progress was good but English has stopped improving — often around B1 or grade 5 to 7.

What you needA center that can identify the specific blocker (vocabulary depth, writing structure, academic vs conversational English) and address it directly.

03

The transitioning child

The family is moving into the international school system from another school context.

What you needA calibrated bridging program with experience preparing children for the target school's entrance assessment and curriculum.

04

The exam-pressured child

IGCSE, IB English or IELTS is approaching.

What you needA center that knows the specific exam in depth and balances exam technique with genuine language work.

05

The reluctant or anxious child

Emotional resistance to English class, refusal to read, freezing in oral assessments.

What you needA small-group setting that feels safe, teachers who understand affective barriers to language learning, and patience.

Not sure which one?

A 60–90 minute free assessment across five skill areas tells you where your child actually sits.

What is your timeline?

  • 12 months out from a target (university entrance, IGCSE, school transfer) — you can work systematically.
  • 3 months out — you need an intensive program with a specialist center, not a generalist.
  • Open-ended supplementary support — prioritize fit over speed.

What is your budget?

  • Quality tuition in HCMC runs from roughly 200,000 VND per session (private tutor, lower end) to 800,000 VND+ for specialist small-group instruction.
  • Over a year of twice-weekly sessions the difference is significant. Cheaper usually means larger classes, less qualified teachers or thinner curriculum.
  • Decide what you can sustain over a full school year, not one term.

Step 2

Understand Your Three Real Options

Most international school families in HCMC end up choosing between three options. Each has clear strengths and clear trade-offs. The marketing language obscures these. Here is the honest version.

e.g. ILA, Apollo, VUS, British Council, Wall Street English

Strengths

  • Established, wide footprint, well-known brand
  • Consistent (if generic) curriculum
  • Accessible mass-market pricing
  • Good for general exposure and conversational fluency
  • Decent IELTS prep for adults and older teens

Trade-offs

  • Classes of 8 to 15 students
  • Teachers are generalists, not international-school curriculum specialists
  • Built for general English progression, not IB / IGCSE demands
  • Differentiation by ability is structurally limited at that size

Right answer when

Your child is in mainstream Vietnamese education or at a bilingual school where English is one subject among many, you want general exposure rather than academic alignment, and class-size differentiation is not a primary concern.

Wrong answer when

Your child is at a fully English-medium international school, has been at the chain for over a year and progress has slowed, is preparing for a specific exam pathway, or needs differentiated instruction.

e.g. Spark, Everest Education, The Edge, Intertu, ITG

Strengths

  • Smaller classes, typically 4 to 8
  • Teachers are specialists in particular curriculum areas
  • Curriculum built for international school families
  • Diagnostic assessment and differentiated grouping
  • Closer teacher–student–parent relationship

Trade-offs

  • Higher cost per session than chains
  • Smaller footprint, often single-location
  • Less scheduling flexibility
  • Quality varies — not every "small-group specialist" delivers on the promise

Right answer when

Your child is at an international or bilingual school, the work needs to align to academic English and curriculum demands, individual feedback density matters, and you can sustain the higher per-session cost.

Wrong answer when

You need a multi-branch footprint, your child is in mainstream Vietnamese education, or the budget cannot support specialist pricing.

Independent tutors, usually found by word of mouth

Strengths

  • Maximum individual attention
  • Schedule flexibility, often at home
  • The right tutor can be transformative for a specific need

Trade-offs

  • No peer dynamic — children acquire language partly from other children
  • Quality varies enormously and is hard to evaluate
  • Highest cost per hour of the three
  • No curriculum coherence; hard to cover all skills with one tutor

Right answer when

A specific narrow need (early dyslexia work, advanced acceleration, exam-specific coaching), a child who cannot tolerate group settings for a documented reason, or a short-term intensive intervention.

Wrong answer when

General English development across all skills, where the absence of peers becomes a liability — or when "expensive equals best" thinking overrides the structural advantages of a small group.

Step 3

The Evaluation Framework

When you have shortlisted two or three options, evaluate them across the seven dimensions that actually matter. The question is not "which has the best marketing" but "which structurally delivers what my child needs."

1Class sizeAsk the actual maximum, not the average.

Many centers advertise "small classes" and mean 8 to 12. Some mean 15. Six is the threshold above which differentiated instruction becomes structurally difficult: a teacher cannot reliably hear every child speak in every session or give meaningful written feedback on every piece of work. We have a separate piece on the research behind this. A center that hedges or gives a range is telling you something.

2Teacher specialismWho specifically will teach my child?

What are their specific qualifications? Are they an IB specialist? An IGCSE specialist? A phonics specialist? Have they worked in international school environments? "Native speaker" is not a qualification. "TEFL certified" is a baseline, not a specialism.

3Diagnostic processHow do you assess my child before placing them?

A serious center assesses across multiple skill areas (reading age, writing, speaking, listening, vocabulary) before recommending placement. If a center wants to enroll without a real diagnostic, their grouping is by registration date rather than by ability. Fine for some children, a problem for others — know which you are choosing.

4Curriculum alignmentHow does your curriculum align to my child's school?

A center using generic textbooks is not aligned to anything specific. A center that can name the IB English specification, the IGCSE English Language curriculum or the Cambridge Young Learners progression is doing curriculum work that compounds.

5Progress reportingHow often, how detailed, which skills?

Vague summary feedback is a sign the center is not measuring outcomes. Detailed reports across multiple skills, every six to eight weeks, with specific observations, show the underlying assessment work is being done.

6Trial class or assessmentUse it — and watch.

Look for how much speaking time your child gets, how the teacher gives feedback, how the class is structured, whether there is differentiation between students. Children are unreliable about whether they "liked" a class but reliable about whether they understood it.

7Pricing transparencyAsk for the full pricing in writing.

Annual, term and per-session. What is included, what is extra, what the cancellation terms are. Almost no English center in HCMC publishes prices — a category-wide failure of trust. Treat willingness to be transparent about pricing as a signal of how the center treats parents in general.

Red flags worth taking seriously

None of these alone is disqualifying, but combined they should slow you down.

  • Promised band scores or grades. No center can promise an IELTS 8.0 or an IB 7. The honest version is measurable progress over an appropriate timeframe.
  • Hedging on class size, credentials or pricing. A center that hedges on basic questions is hedging on the questions that matter.
  • Pressure tactics. "Sign up today for a discount." "Only two spaces left." Specialist centers do not need scarcity tactics.
  • Generic curriculum claims. "We follow international standards" is not a curriculum. Naming Cambridge YLE, IGCSE and IB specifications is.
  • No progress measurement. If they cannot say how progress is measured over six months, it is not being measured.
  • Too-good-to-be-true pricing. Specialist small-group at chain prices means bigger classes, less qualified teachers or a thinner curriculum. Pick which.

Self-Assessment

What to Ask Before Booking Anywhere

Save this list and ask each center on your shortlist the same ten questions. The answers will sort the options faster than any marketing comparison.

A center that answers clearly, specifically and without hedging is operating at a professional level. A center that struggles with these questions is one to walk away from, regardless of how good the marketing is.

Print this checklist

Ten questions

  1. What is the maximum class size? Not the average — the cap.
  2. Who specifically will teach my child, and what is their qualification, specialism and international-school experience?
  3. How do you assess my child before placing them in a class?
  4. How does your curriculum align to my child's school requirements (IB PYP / MYP / DP, IGCSE, IPC)?
  5. How often will I receive progress reports, and which skills do you track separately?
  6. Can I observe a class before enrolling?
  7. What is the full pricing in writing, including extras?
  8. What is the cancellation policy if my child needs to stop?
  9. What outcomes can you show from previous students with a similar profile?
  10. What happens if my child is not progressing as expected?

Where Spark Fits

Since we have written this whole guide, you have a fair right to ask where Spark sits on it. Here is the honest version: Spark is a specialist small-group center in Thao Dien — Option 2 above.

We are not the right answer for every family. We are not in District 7. We are not the cheapest center. We are not designed for general English among families with no international school exposure — ILA and Apollo do that better than we do. And we are deliberately small, so we cannot fit every schedule request.

We are the right answer when an international or bilingual school family in or near Thao Dien wants serious English work done seriously, and structural fit matters more than convenience or lowest cost.

Spark on the seven criteria

  • Class size — hard cap of six.
  • Teacher specialism — English specialists with international school experience.
  • Diagnostic — five skill areas assessed separately.
  • Curriculum — CEFR-aligned through Cambridge YLE, IGCSE, IB English, IELTS.
  • Progress reports — every six weeks.
  • Trial — free 60–90 minute assessment, no obligation.
  • Pricing — published transparently.

FAQs

Frequently asked questions about choosing an English center in HCMC

What is the most important factor when choosing an English center for an international school child?

Class size. Everything else (teacher quality, curriculum, progress reporting) flows from class size structurally. A great teacher in a class of fifteen cannot deliver the same individual attention and differentiation as a competent teacher in a class of six. Class size sets the ceiling on what is possible. Other factors raise or lower the level within that ceiling.

Should I choose the closest English center or travel further for a better fit?

Within reason, fit beats convenience. Twice-weekly sessions over an academic year is roughly 80 to 100 sessions. Better-fit instruction across that volume produces meaningfully better outcomes than mediocre instruction. That said, if travel adds an hour each way, schedule strain often kills consistency. The sweet spot is the best-fit center within a reasonable commute. For families in Thao Dien and the surrounding international school community, that often means a Thao Dien-based specialist.

Is a more expensive center always better?

No. Some expensive centers are over-priced for what they deliver. Some moderately priced centers are excellent. The pricing is a signal but not a proxy for quality. Use the framework above (class size, teacher specialism, diagnostic process, curriculum alignment, progress reporting) to evaluate, then check whether the pricing matches the value those structural factors deliver.

How do I know if my child is making real progress at an English center?

Two ways. First, the center should give you specific progress measurements every six to eight weeks across multiple skills (reading age, writing development, vocabulary, listening, speaking). Vague "improving nicely" feedback is not measurement. Second, look for transfer effects: is your child's school work in English-medium subjects improving? Are their school reports getting stronger? Real English progress shows up in school outcomes within two to three terms, not just in center-internal assessments.

Should I switch English centers if my child is not progressing?

First, ask the center directly: why is my child not progressing, and what would change? A serious center will give you a specific diagnostic answer. If the answer is vague, switch. If the answer is specific and the proposed change makes sense, give it one term to work. If the change does not produce measurable progress, switch. Sticking with a center out of inertia or sunk cost rarely produces a different outcome.

Are online English programs (Cambly, Preply, online tutors) a good alternative to a center?

For some specific needs, yes. Online tutors can be excellent for additional speaking practice or for short-term exam-specific coaching. They are usually less effective for systematic curriculum-aligned development across multiple skills, and they offer no peer dynamic. The right answer is often a combination: a primary in-person program with structure, plus targeted online support for specific needs.

My child has been at ILA for three years and I'm not sure they need to switch. How do I decide?

Ask: are they making the progress you expected when you enrolled? If yes, stay. If no, ask the center directly what is causing the slowdown and what they plan to change. If the answer is satisfying, give it one term. If the answer is unsatisfying or progress continues to stall, look at specialist alternatives. Many international school families come to Spark after exactly this period at a chain center and we can usually identify the specific blocker quickly.

What about reviews online? Are they reliable?

Use them carefully. Specific, detailed reviews from clearly identifiable parents are useful. Vague positive reviews and vague negative reviews are not. Where possible, ask other parents in your child's school community directly. Word of mouth in international school parent groups is more reliable than online review aggregators.

How do I know if a small-group center is actually delivering on its small-group claim?

Ask to observe a class. If they decline, that is a signal. If they agree, watch the actual class size, watch how the teacher gives feedback, watch how each child is engaged. A small group that is actually a small group will look different from a large class with a "small group" label.

When should I start looking for outside English support?

Earlier than parents typically do. The most common pattern we see is parents waiting until a school report flags an issue, by which time the gap has been there for at least a term or two. If you notice early signals (reading age dropping, writing not developing, speaking confidence dropping), it is worth doing a free assessment to know where things stand. Better to act when the gap is small than when it has compounded.

Where can I get more help thinking through this decision?

Our free assessment includes a structured conversation about your child's specific situation, what kind of support they actually need, and whether Spark is the right fit. The assessment is genuinely diagnostic; we will tell you honestly if our recommendation is to look elsewhere. Book at sparkvn.com/Assessment.

In short

The S.P.A.R.K. framework at a glance

  • S — Systematic Instruction: learning built step by step.
  • P — Personalized Learning: every learner is different.
  • A — Academic Language: moving beyond conversational English.
  • R — Reading Mastery: the foundation of academic success.
  • K — Knowledge Building: building understanding of the world.

At Spark, we believe that strong outcomes are not the result of luck, talent, or simply spending more time in class. Real progress comes from a clear educational philosophy, evidence-based teaching practices, and a consistent approach to learning.

That is why every lesson, program, and learning pathway at Spark is guided by our S.P.A.R.K. framework.

The Spark Method combines five essential elements that support long-term literacy, language development, and academic success.

Together, these principles help students become confident readers, capable writers, effective communicators, and independent learners.

What Is the S.P.A.R.K. Framework?

Learning Built Step by Step

Students learn best when new knowledge is introduced in a logical sequence.

Rather than teaching isolated skills or jumping randomly between topics, Spark follows structured learning pathways that build understanding gradually over time.

Each new skill is connected to previous learning, allowing students to strengthen existing knowledge while developing new abilities.

For example:

  • Sounds are taught before words.
  • Words are taught before sentences.
  • Sentences are taught before paragraphs.
  • Paragraphs are taught before essays.

This systematic approach reduces confusion, improves retention, and helps students develop confidence as they experience success at every stage of learning.

What Parents Notice

Students become less reliant on guessing and develop a stronger understanding of how language works.

Every Learner Is Different

No two students arrive with the same strengths, challenges, experiences, or goals.

Some students need support with reading fluency. Others require help organizing ideas in writing. Some may have strong speaking skills but limited academic vocabulary.

At Spark, instruction is adapted to meet individual needs.

Teachers continuously monitor progress and adjust support based on each student's development.

Personalization may include:

  • Individual learning goals
  • Differentiated activities
  • Targeted feedback
  • Additional support in specific skill areas
  • Adjusted pacing when necessary

This ensures that students receive the right level of challenge while continuing to experience success.

What Parents Notice

Students receive support that addresses their specific needs rather than following a one-size-fits-all approach.

Moving Beyond Conversational English

Many students can communicate comfortably in everyday situations but struggle when faced with academic tasks.

They may understand conversations yet find it difficult to:

  • Read complex texts
  • Write detailed responses
  • Explain their thinking
  • Use subject-specific vocabulary
  • Participate in academic discussions

Academic success requires a different type of language.

At Spark, students learn the vocabulary, sentence structures, and communication skills needed for school, examinations, and future academic study.

The Foundation of Academic Success

Reading is one of the strongest predictors of educational achievement.

Students who read well generally learn more efficiently, acquire vocabulary more quickly, write more effectively, and perform better across a wide range of subjects.

That is why reading sits at the center of the Spark Method.

Reading instruction extends beyond simply recognizing words on a page.

Students develop:

  • Phonics and decoding skills
  • Reading accuracy
  • Reading fluency
  • Vocabulary knowledge
  • Reading comprehension
  • Critical reading skills
  • Analytical thinking

As students grow, reading becomes a tool for learning rather than a barrier to learning.

Strong readers become stronger learners.

What Parents Notice

Students become more confident readers, tackle challenging texts more independently, and engage more actively with learning.

Building Understanding of the World

Reading and writing skills are important, but students also need knowledge.

The more students know about the world, the easier it becomes for them to understand new information, make connections, and think critically.

At Spark, students engage with a wide range of topics, texts, and ideas that expand their background knowledge while strengthening literacy skills.

Students may explore:

  • Science topics
  • Historical events
  • Literature
  • Current issues
  • Cultural perspectives
  • Real-world problems

This approach helps students develop curiosity, confidence, and the ability to engage thoughtfully with complex ideas.

Knowledge supports comprehension, and comprehension supports learning.

What Parents Notice

Students become more curious, ask deeper questions, and demonstrate stronger understanding when discussing new topics.

pages.title: Class Size
pages.excerpt: Spark's small classes give every student personalised attention, confidence, and an active role in learning.
pages.content:
In short

Class size, in numbers

  • 8–10 minutes of individual speaking time per child in a class of 6 — versus 2.5–3 minutes in a class of 20.
  • ~1,000 corrections per school year in a small class, versus roughly 200 in a large one.
  • Below about 8 students every child speaks in every session; above 15, most are effectively silent.
  • Spark caps every class at six — a hard cap, not an average.

If you are evaluating English centers for your child, class size is the single most important structural question you can ask. Not the curriculum. Not the brand name. Not the price. The number of students in the room sets the ceiling on everything else: how much your child speaks, how much feedback they receive, how quickly a teacher spots a misunderstanding, and how fast your child actually progresses.

This is not opinion. It is structural. A teacher with twenty students and a teacher with six students are doing fundamentally different jobs, regardless of how good either teacher is. The teacher with twenty students is managing a room. The teacher with six students is teaching children.

This page explains why class size matters specifically for English language learning (not just education in general), what the research actually shows, where the critical thresholds are, and why Spark caps every class at six students. It is written for parents of international and bilingual school children in HCMC who are comparing options and want to understand the structural differences between them, not just the marketing.

The Basic Math

Speaking Time, Feedback Density, and Error Correction

Language learning is not like learning math or history. You cannot learn a language by listening. You learn by producing language, making mistakes, and having those mistakes corrected in real time. This is well established in second language acquisition research and is the foundation of communicative language teaching. The implication for class size is direct and mathematical.

Speaking Time

In a 90-minute English session, a teacher needs to explain, demonstrate, and manage transitions. In practice, roughly 50 to 60 minutes of a session involve student production: speaking, writing, reading aloud, or answering questions. In a class of 20 students, that is roughly 2.5 to 3 minutes of individual speaking time per child. In a class of 6, it is 8 to 10 minutes. This is not a marginal difference. It is a threefold increase in the single most important activity for language acquisition.

For a child who is shy, or who is at a lower level than their peers, 2.5 minutes is often zero. They can sit through an entire session in a large class without producing a single sentence, and neither the teacher nor the parent may know. In a class of six, the teacher hears every child, every session. There is nowhere to hide, and no child needs to.

Feedback Density

Feedback density is the number of corrections, suggestions, and targeted comments a teacher can give each student per session. In writing, it is the difference between reading every sentence a child writes and skimming a paragraph. In speaking, it is the difference between correcting a grammar error in the moment and letting it pass because there are nineteen other hands up.

In a class of 20, a teacher might give each child two or three meaningful corrections per session. In a class of 6, that number rises to ten or fifteen. Over a school year of 80 sessions, the difference compounds dramatically: roughly 200 corrections in a large class versus 1,000 in a small one. This is not a subtle pedagogical nuance. It is a five-times difference in the volume of targeted feedback a child receives.

Error Correction Timing

There is a window in language learning called the "correction window." When a child makes an error, the most effective correction happens within seconds, while the child still remembers what they said and why. In a large class, errors pass uncorrected because the teacher is attending to someone else. In a small class, the teacher catches the error in the moment, corrects it, and the child integrates the correction immediately.

This matters more than parents typically realize. Uncorrected errors become habits. A child who says "I have been to there" three hundred times without correction will find it significantly harder to unlearn than a child who was corrected the first or second time. Small classes are not just more pleasant. They are structurally different in how they handle the mechanics of language acquisition.

What The Research Actually Says

Parents deserve to know that the research on class size is more nuanced than either side of the debate typically presents. The honest summary is this: reducing class size from 25 to 20 produces small, inconsistent effects. Reducing class size from 15 to 8, or from 8 to 4, produces meaningful and consistent effects, particularly for younger children and children from non-English-speaking backgrounds.

The STAR Study

The most cited class-size research is the Tennessee STAR study (Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio), conducted across 79 schools from 1985 to 1989. It compared classes of 13 to 17 students (small) against classes of 22 to 25 students (regular). The findings showed statistically significant improvements in reading for students in smaller classes, with the strongest effects in the early grades and among minority and low-income students. The gains persisted into later years even after students returned to regular-sized classes.

The STAR study is important but has a limitation for our context: its "small" classes were 13 to 17 students, which is still larger than what specialist English centers offer. The study tells us that reducing class size matters. It does not tell us much about what happens below 10 students, which is where the most interesting effects for language learning occur.

The Language-Specific Research

Language learning benefits disproportionately from small classes compared to other subjects. This is because language acquisition requires production and feedback, not just comprehension. Several studies in the second language acquisition literature have documented this.

The relationship between class size and oral participation is not linear. It follows a threshold pattern. Below about 8 students, every child speaks in every session. Between 8 and 15, participation drops to roughly half the class. Above 15, a small number of confident students dominate and the rest are effectively silent. For English as a second or additional language, where oral production is essential to progress, this threshold effect means that classes above 8 students are structurally limiting for the quieter half of the room.

Writing feedback follows a similar pattern. A teacher can read and provide detailed feedback on writing from 6 students in a 90-minute session. They cannot do the same for 15. At best, they skim. The child receives a tick or a grade, not the sentence-level correction that drives improvement.

The Honest Caveats

The research also shows that class size alone is not sufficient. A small class with a poor teacher does not outperform a large class with an excellent teacher. Class size sets the ceiling; teacher quality determines where within that ceiling the outcomes fall. This is why Spark combines small class size with specialist teaching. Neither alone is enough.

There is also a floor below which smaller classes stop adding value for typical learners. One-on-one instruction removes the peer dynamic that helps children acquire language through interaction, modeling, and social motivation. A child alone with a teacher does not hear other children making and correcting mistakes, does not practice the turn-taking and listening that group communication requires, and does not benefit from the "eavesdropping effect" where they learn from corrections given to a peer. The research on language learning in particular suggests that 3 to 6 students is the range where both individual attention and peer dynamics are fully present.

The Six-Student Threshold

Why Spark Chose Six

The number six is not arbitrary. It is the result of a specific set of structural requirements that we believe are non-negotiable for effective English language instruction.

At six students, a teacher can hear every child read aloud in every session. This matters for phonics, for reading comprehension, and for identifying decoding errors that a child might mask in a larger group by mumbling or staying silent.

At six students, a teacher can read every piece of writing carefully and provide detailed, sentence-level feedback. Not "good work" or a grade, but specific comments: "This sentence needs a conjunction," "Your vocabulary here is strong but the tense is wrong," "Try restructuring this paragraph with the topic sentence first."

At six students, a teacher can correct speaking errors in real time, in the correction window, without losing the attention of the rest of the group. Beyond six, the teacher begins to choose between correcting the speaker and managing the group. That choice is the structural moment where large-class teaching diverges from small-class teaching.

At six students, diagnostic grouping works. The teacher can hold in mind the specific profile of each child: where they are strong, where they are weak, what they need next. Beyond six, the profiles begin to blur and teaching shifts from individual responsiveness to group management.

At six students, shy or anxious children participate. The social pressure of a larger group keeps many children silent. In a group of six, the social dynamic shifts from "audience and performers" to "conversation among peers." This is particularly important for children who are already anxious about their English.

We have experimented with groups of eight and found that the quality of feedback begins to degrade. We have worked with groups of four and found that the peer dynamic is thinner. Six is the number where both individual feedback and group dynamics are fully present. It is not the cheapest structure to deliver. It is the most effective one.

What This Means For Parents Comparing English Centers

When you ask an English center "what is your class size," listen carefully to the answer. There are three common patterns in HCMC.

The large chains (ILA, Apollo, VUS, British Council, Wall Street English) typically run classes of 8 to 15 students. Some advertise "small classes" and mean 10 to 12. These class sizes are effective for general English exposure and conversation practice, but they structurally limit the individual feedback, error correction, and speaking time that academic English requires.

Specialist centers vary. Some cap at 6. Some cap at 8. Some advertise "small groups" without specifying a number. Ask for the maximum, not the average. A center that says "our average class size is 6" may have some classes of 10 and some of 3. The maximum tells you the worst case your child will experience.

Private one-on-one tutors give maximum individual attention but zero peer dynamic. For language learning specifically, this trade-off is real.

FAQs

Frequently asked questions about class size and English learning

Does class size really matter that much, or is teacher quality more important?

Both matter, but they interact. A great teacher in a class of 20 is constrained by the math: they cannot give each child enough speaking time, writing feedback, or real-time correction. A mediocre teacher in a class of 6 still gives more individual attention than most teachers can in a class of 20. The ideal is a great teacher in a small class. Class size sets the ceiling; teacher quality determines how close you get to it.

My child is at ILA and seems to enjoy it. Should I switch to a smaller class?

Not necessarily. If your child is making the progress you expected and the goals are conversational rather than academic, a chain center may be the right fit. The class size question becomes critical when your child needs targeted academic English development, structured writing improvement, or IELTS preparation where every error corrected matters.

Is one-on-one tutoring better than a small group?

For language learning, usually not. One-on-one removes the peer dynamic that is particularly important for language acquisition: hearing other children speak, practicing turn-taking, learning from peers' mistakes, and the social motivation of a small group. One-on-one is valuable for very specific needs (dyslexia support, advanced acceleration, short-term exam coaching), but for ongoing English development, a small group of 4 to 6 is structurally stronger.

What does "small class" mean at Spark?

Maximum six students. This is a hard cap, not an average. We do not add a seventh student to an existing class. If a class is full at six, we open a new group or place the child on a waitlist until a suitable group forms.

Why not cap at four instead of six?

Groups of four work well but produce a thinner peer dynamic. With four students, the conversational range narrows and the interaction patterns become less varied. Six gives enough social complexity for genuine group communication while still allowing full individual attention.

My child is shy. Will a small group help or make things worse?

Almost always better. Shy children in large classes often go silent because the social risk of speaking in front of 15 or 20 peers is too high. In a group of six, the dynamic is conversational rather than performative. Shy children begin speaking within weeks, often surprising their parents.

How does class size affect IELTS preparation specifically?

IELTS requires precision in writing and fluency in speaking, both of which depend on high-frequency error correction and extensive practice. In a class of 15, a student might write one practice essay per session and receive general feedback. In a class of six, they write the same essay and receive sentence-level correction across grammar, vocabulary, coherence, and task achievement. This is one of the reasons over 95% of Joe Evans' IELTS students at Spark achieve Band 7.5 or higher.

  • Free assessment of 60 to 90 minutes across five skill areas, no obligation to enroll.

About the Community

Thao Dien is not just a neighborhood. For international school families in Ho Chi Minh City, it is the center of gravity. Within a radius of roughly two kilometers from Spark English Center, there are more international and bilingual schools per square kilometer than anywhere else in Vietnam.

Spark was built in Thao Dien, for Thao Dien families, because this is where the need is most concentrated and most specific. We are not a chain that happened to open a branch here. We are a specialist English center that exists because the international school community in this neighborhood needs something that the broader English center market does not provide: small-class, curriculum-aligned, academically rigorous English support delivered within walking distance of the schools where these children spend their days.

The Thao Dien School Cluster

British International School HCMC (BIS)

Location: 225 Nguyen Van Huong, Thao Dien. Curriculum: British (IGCSE, A-Levels), part of Nord Anglia Education. Approximately 1,800 students from 50+ nationalities.

English demands

BIS follows the British curriculum with structured assessment through IGCSE and A-Levels. Academic English requirements are high from Year 3 onward, with extended writing, reading comprehension, and analytical thinking central to the assessment framework.

Where Spark helps

Students in EAL who need faster progress. Students preparing for IGCSE English. Students whose writing has plateaued at B1. Students who need IELTS for university applications alongside A-Level work.

International School of Ho Chi Minh City (ISHCMC)

Location: 28 Vo Truong Toan, An Phu Ward. Curriculum: IB (PYP, MYP, DP), one of the longest-established IB World Schools in Vietnam. 1,200+ students from 50+ nationalities.

English demands

The IB's inquiry-based approach places heavy demands on academic English: students must read critically, write analytically, and express complex ideas orally from early in the MYP. IB English Language and Literature at DP level requires C1 English.

Where Spark helps

Students transitioning from PYP to MYP who need stronger academic writing. Students preparing for IB English. Students whose English is conversationally strong but academically behind.

European International School HCMC (EIS)

Location: 730 F-G-K Le Van Mien, Thao Dien. Curriculum: IB (PYP, MYP, DP) in a smaller, village-style campus.

Where Spark helps

Similar profile to ISHCMC families. The smaller school environment means less EAL resource internally, which makes outside support more relevant for students who need it.

Australian International School Saigon (AIS)

Location: 36 Thao Dien Road (Thao Dien campus), plus Thu Thiem and Xi campuses. Curriculum: Australian pathway with IGCSE and IB Diploma options. 1,100+ students from 40+ nationalities.

Where Spark helps

Students navigating the IGCSE/IB pathway choice who need English strong enough for either option. Students at the Thao Dien campus who need after-school support within the neighborhood.

Aurora International School

Location: 11-13 Tran Ngoc Dien, Thao Dien. Curriculum: Reggio Emilia-inspired early years, New Zealand curriculum for primary and middle school.

Where Spark helps

Children transitioning from Reggio-inspired early years into structured primary. Families preparing for a transition to BIS, ISHCMC, or another school at Year 7. Children who need systematic phonics development.

EtonHouse International Pre-School Thao Dien

Location: 42 Street 10, Thao Dien. Curriculum: Reggio Emilia-inspired, IB PYP candidate.

Where Spark helps

Phonics and early literacy development before or alongside the transition to primary school. Children who need structured reading and writing foundations.

Other schools in the wider District 2 and Thu Duc area

Beyond the Thao Dien core, we serve families from the American School (TAS), BVIS, Anne Hill, Saint Ange, La Petite Ecole, Saigon Star, Renaissance, ABC International School, and the network of bilingual schools across District 2 including Vinschool and Asian School campuses.

Why a Single Specialist Center Beats a Chain With Branches

There is a reason Spark has one center in Thao Dien and not five branches across HCMC. The reason is quality control.

When an English center opens multiple branches, it needs to staff them. That means hiring more teachers, often at speed, often accepting a lower qualification threshold. The curriculum gets diluted as new staff interpret it differently. Quality varies between branches, and parents have no way to know which branch is strong and which is stretched.

Spark operates differently. We have one location, one teaching team, one consistent standard. Every student is taught by the same small group of specialist teachers. Every parent can speak directly to the director. Every class runs at the same standard because there is no second location where standards might slip.

Our center at 204B7/12 Nguyen Van Huong is within walking distance or a short drive of every school listed above. For most Thao Dien families, the commute is less than ten minutes.

FAQs

What Thao Dien Families Ask us Most

My child goes to BIS/ISHCMC/AIS. Do they really need outside English support?

Sometimes yes, sometimes no. International schools have excellent EAL programs, but those programs serve large numbers of children with diverse needs. If your child has been in EAL for more than a year and progress has slowed, or if their academic English is not keeping pace with curriculum demands, outside support is worth investigating. Our free assessment gives you an honest answer. We have turned families away when school EAL alone was sufficient.

We just moved to Thao Dien. My child starts at BIS/ISHCMC next term. What should we do now?

Book an assessment immediately. The window between arriving in HCMC and starting at a new school is the most valuable time for English preparation. We run intensive bridging programs designed for this exact situation.

My child is at a bilingual school. Is Spark for international school families only?

No. We serve families from bilingual schools (Vinschool, VAS, Asian School, Wellspring, and others) across HCMC. The English needs are different: bilingual school families typically need stronger academic English to complement what the school provides, and many are preparing for a future transition to an international school or for IELTS.

We live in District 7. Is it worth the commute to Thao Dien?

For some families, yes. If the structural advantages of Spark matter enough to justify a 25-to-40 minute commute, the fit can be worth the travel. For families where convenience is a higher priority, we would honestly suggest looking at options closer to home. Better to attend consistently at a good local center than to attend inconsistently at a distant specialist one.

Where exactly is Spark located?

204B7/12 Nguyen Van Huong, Thao Dien Ward, Thu Duc City, Ho Chi Minh City. We are on the main Nguyen Van Huong road, within walking distance of BIS and the surrounding residential developments.

What are Spark's operating hours?

Classes run Monday through Saturday. Most after-school sessions run from 3:00 PM to 8:30 PM on weekdays, with morning and afternoon sessions on Saturdays. We offer flexible scheduling to accommodate the varied dismissal times of different international schools.

Do you coordinate with my child's school?

We work alongside schools, not against them. Our teachers are familiar with the curricula at BIS, ISHCMC, EIS, AIS, and the bilingual schools. We do not contact schools directly unless a parent asks us to, but we welcome parents sharing our progress reports with their child's school teacher.

How do I get started?

Book a free assessment at sparkvn.com/Assessment. The assessment takes 60 to 90 minutes, provides a detailed profile of your child's English across five skill areas, and includes a recommendation for program and placement. There is no obligation to enroll.

FAQs

We understand that parents may have questions before booking an assessment. Here are some of the most common questions about our assessment process, class placement, and student support.

How long does the assessment take?

Most assessments take around 30–45 minutes, depending on the student's age and English level. During this time, our teachers guide students through speaking, reading, phonics, and listening activities in a calm and supportive environment.

Does my child need to prepare?

No preparation is needed before the assessment. We want children to feel relaxed and comfortable so we can see their natural English ability and confidence level during the session.

Will parents receive feedback?

Yes. After the assessment, parents receive personalized feedback about their child's strengths, areas for improvement, and recommended class placement. Our team is also happy to answer questions and discuss the next steps for learning.

Is the assessment stressful?

Not at all. Our teachers create a friendly and encouraging environment designed to help students feel comfortable and confident. The activities are interactive and supportive rather than formal or intimidating.

What ages do you assess?

We assess a wide range of learners, including young children, teenagers, and adult students. Each assessment is adjusted based on the student's age, learning needs, and current English level.

What skills are included in the assessment?

Our assessments may include speaking, pronunciation, reading, phonics, listening, grammar, and comprehension activities. The exact activities are adjusted based on the student's age and English level.

How will I know which class is right for my child?

After the assessment, our teachers recommend a class based on your child's current ability, confidence level, and learning needs. We aim to place students in an environment where they can feel supported while continuing to grow.

Can shy or nervous students still complete the assessment?

Absolutely. Many students feel shy at first, especially when speaking English with a new teacher. Our teachers are experienced in helping children feel relaxed, encouraged, and comfortable throughout the session.

Is the assessment online or in person?

Assessments may be offered in person or online depending on availability and student needs. Our team will help you choose the option that is most convenient and comfortable for your child.

What happens after the assessment?

After the assessment, our team will discuss the results with you and recommend the most suitable class for your child. We will also explain your child's strengths, areas for improvement, and the next steps to help them continue building confidence in English.

Ask a Teacher is Spark's parent advice center.

Ask Your Question

Ask Your Question
